_README: 🔴 THE CORE OF THE PRODUCT. No federal EXPENDITURE file — the MEPS event files, HCUP, CMS claims — carries a dollar or a row for any of these, because those files record care that was DELIVERED AND BILLED: a person who wanted care and did not get it is invisible in all of them, by construction. Two of the six are billed and still invisible, which is worse: a dismissal and care aimed at the wrong target appear in the data as ordinary delivered care, so the money is counted and the fact is not. And the absence is not total: the MEPS household survey does ask separately whether a person was unable to get care or delayed it — access-to-care items ride on the Full Year Consolidated file (AHRQ, MEPS HC-243, 2022) — which is a national count of unmet need, carrying no dollar figure and no account of one person's search. Dr. John Phillips named this exact gap at the 2026-08-20 office hours: 'a lot of the things that will be showing up on patient need come from individuals who have actually received service of some way, shape or form. And a neat thing about this is the potential to identify folks who want service, but don't get it. And so that I think is going to be the... data challenge.' This file turns that data challenge into the thing the tool measures.

categories.label: Care you needed and did not seek
categories.prompt: Was there care you knew you needed but did not go and get?
categories.whyInvisible: A visit that never happened generates no claim, no encounter record and no survey event. In every federal expenditure file this looks identical to being well.

categories.label: Care you asked for and were refused
categories.prompt: Did a clinician or insurer refuse something you asked for?
categories.whyInvisible: A denial is recorded by the payer, not in expenditure data, and a clinician declining to order a test leaves no trace at all. The need existed and is uncounted.

categories.label: Times you were told it was nothing
categories.prompt: How many times were you told your symptoms were anxiety, stress, or nothing at all?
examples: told it was in my head
told to come back if it got worse
categories.whyInvisible: The visit is billed, so it appears in the data as care delivered. What the data cannot show is that it produced no answer. A dismissal and a diagnosis cost the same and look the same in an expenditure file.

categories.label: Care aimed at the wrong thing
categories.prompt: Were you treated for something you did not have?
categories.whyInvisible: This care is fully recorded and fully paid, and it is counted as successful utilization. Nothing in the data marks it as care that was aimed at the wrong target.

categories.label: Time spent searching rather than being treated
categories.prompt: Roughly how long from your first symptom to an answer?
categories.whyInvisible: Federal expenditure files have no field for duration of an undiagnosed period. The clock only starts when a code is assigned — so the longest and most expensive part of an odyssey begins after the data starts counting.

categories.label: What the search cost you outside of medicine
categories.prompt: What did this take from you that no bill records?
categories.whyInvisible: No health dataset has a field for this. It is the largest cost most people in a diagnostic odyssey report, and it is the one no federal file has ever counted.

weighting._note: 🔴 PHILLIPS'S SIGNATURE PROBE, asked as the FIRST question of the 2026-08-20 session and returned to three more times: 'whether it be doing something to kind of get a sense from the affected communities about the things that matter most, finding ways of waiting [weighting] would be... really fantastic and a great contribution.' This is that. Weights are ELICITED from the affected community, never assigned by us, never modelled. We report what people said and how many said it.
weighting.question: Of everything this search cost you, which hurt the most?
weighting.instruction: Rank as many as you want. There is no right answer and nothing here is scored.
weighting.reportedAs: A frequency distribution across respondents, with the count. Never a weighted index we invented.
